The neat thing about Garmins in general is that you really don’t need the latest models to get the most out of the company’s platform. articles.title: Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
articles.summary: Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success.
body: “Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It's the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.”

Like many other entrants in the World Endurance Championship’s Hypercar class, Ford has chosen the rear-wheel-drive LMDh technical approach rather than building the GT41 entirely from scratch, as Ferrari and Aston Martin do with their cars. LMDh cars start with one of four approved carbon fiber chassis—in this case, Ford is working with Oreca, which has also partnered with Genesis and Acura.

articles.title: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?
articles.summary: The pay is good and there's lots of work, so what's behind the shortage of elevator mechanics?
body: Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here.

When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again.
"They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?"

The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started."
points: The pay is good and there's lots of work, so what's behind the shortage of elevator mechanics?

articles.title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
articles.summary: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO 2 emissions.
body: A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO 2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO 2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO 2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.
points: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems.
But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO 2 emissions.

articles.title: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
articles.summary: Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.
body: As an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.

I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).

Accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.
My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.

articles.summary: Android Auto is now smarter than before, thanks to the addition of Gemini. You can navigate more easily and even bounce ideas off of it along the way.
body: Google Assistant is being replaced by Google’s more advanced Gemini AI across all platforms, and that includes Android Auto. If the switch hasn’t happened yet on your own vehicle’s dashboard, then it should happen soon.
You’ll see a message onscreen announcing the arrival of Gemini, with the new “spark” icon (a small star by a sound-wave-like icon), instead of the traditional microphone when the AI is active.

If you've used Gemini before on your phone, on the web, or somewhere else, then you're going to know the extras that it brings over Google Assistant. It's a truly natural conversation partner that can dig deep into information available online, and respond to a much wider range of queries. Here's what the upgraded app can do specifically when you're traveling on the road.

All of the standard commands you might have already been using are still here, of course, like "navigate home" or “Where's the nearest Walmart?” With Gemini though, there's much more flexibility in what you can say without the AI getting confused or misunderstanding what you're asking about.
